title: Directed assembly of cathode interlayers enables efficient binary organic solar cells - Nature Energy
text:
Download PDF

AbstractCathode interlayers create interfacial dipoles in organic solar cells to maximize device efficiency. However, the dipoles are highly dependent on the molecular orientation of the interlayers, which remain challenging to be controlled. Here, based on the amphiphilic nature of the interlayers, we show a stepwise film deposition approach using a polar solvent for active layer pretreatment and a bipolar solvent for subsequent interlayer self assembly. Sum-frequency generation vibrational spectroscopy reveals a preferred perpendicular orientation of the interlayer molecules, thereby enhancing the surface potential and reducing the charge transport resistance. As a result, we achieve a certified efficiency of 20.65% and fill factor of 82.7% in binary organic solar cells. This method is universally applicable to different cathode interlayers and active layers. Our work highlights the importance of controlling interlayer molecular orientation for unlocking significant performance gains, paving the way for further advancements in device optimization.

Organic Solar Cell Performance Optimization Techniques

MainOrganic solar cells (OSCs) have emerged as a promising renewable energy technology, garnering substantial interest from both academia and industry over the past decade1,2,3. This interest derives largely from their lightweight, flexible and cost-effective nature relative to conventional rigid silicon-based technologies4,5. Recent advancements in material design and device engineering have driven power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) beyond 20%, marking a critical step towards commercial viability6,7,8,9.Cathode interlayers (CILs), positioned between the photoactive layer and the metal cathode, play a pivotal role in improving performance of OSCs via tuning energy band alignment and facilitating charge extraction10,11,12,13,14,15. CILs usually incorporate n-type aromatic cores functionalized with polar groups, such as amines. The polar groups modulate the cathode work function via interfacial dipole formation, whereas the n-type cores reduce contact resistance and optimize energy-level alignment16,17,18,19. This dual functionality enables efficient ohmic contact through selective carrier extraction with minimized recombination12,20. However, complex intermolecular and intramolecular interactions within interlayer molecules often disrupt the optimal interfacial dipole formation, which limits the full potential for advancing device performance.The orientation of interlayer molecules, especially the alignment of aromatic cores, is a key factor governing interfacial dipole formation and, consequently, charge extraction efficiency in OSCs21. Techniques such as vapour deposition can promote edge-on or face-on molecular orientations depending on deposition conditions, while dip coating and the Langmuir–Blodgett method enable some degree of control over molecular packing and alignment at interfaces22,23. However, these methods are primarily effective on well-defined, rigid surfaces and often fail to accommodate the soft, heterogeneous and chemically complex nature of the active layer in OSCs. These limitations, combined with the poor solubility of interlayer materials in orthogonal solvents, leave current approaches insufficient for reliably directing molecular alignment in cathode interlayers.In this Article, we successfully address these challenges by introducing a straightforward yet effective stepwise film deposition process based on the amphiphilic nature of the interlayers, using a polar solvent for active layer pretreatment and a bipolar solvent for subsequent interlayer self assembly. Furthermore, asymmetric S-heterocyclic annulated perylene-diimide (PDI) are synthesized as CILs. This approach promotes the perpendicular orientation of interlayer molecules on the active interlayer surface in OSCs and overcomes the solubility issues associated with alcohol/water-based orthogonal deposition. As a result, we achieve a champion PCE of over 20.7% in binary OSCs. This work not only underscores the importance of interlayer self assembly to control the interfacial dipole but also highlights the potential of tailored interlayers to further advance OSC technology.Materials synthesis and characterizationPDI-based materials are widely studied organic semiconductors, attractive for their green and cost-effective synthesis24,25. In this study, we synthesized two S-heterocyclic annulated PDIs based on the benchmark interlayer of PDINN (an aliphatic amine-functionalized PDI) to regulate their function as cathode interlayer in conventional devices (Fig. 1a)26. The structures of the PDI interlayers are shown in Fig. 1b. The synthesis of the PDIs is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1, with experimental details and characterizations provided in Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Figs. 2–5.Fig. 1: Device architecture and material characterization.Full size imagea, Device structure of organic solar cells. b, Chemical structures of PDI interlayer. The inset depicts a schematic of a PDI molecule, with the PDI core donated by a square and the amine side chains indicated by circles. c, Normalized film absorptions of three PDI-CILs. d, Cyclic voltammograms of three PDI-CILs. e, Line-cut curves from the GIWAXS results. f, Solid-state electron spin resonance spectra of three PDI-CILs.Source dataUltraviolet–visible spectra reveal progressively blue-shifted absorption in thin films, yielding optical gaps of 1.97, 2.07 and 2.19 eV for PDINN, PDISNN and PDI2SNN, respectively (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 6). Cyclic voltammetry (Fig. 1d) shows that both the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy levels shift progressively to lower energies (ELUMO: −3.78, −3.83, −3.85 eV; EHOMO: −6.02, −6.11, −6.14 eV) with increasing S-annelation on the PDI core. The low-lying EHOMO suggests enhanced hole-blocking capability at cathodes. Grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) analysis demonstrates an improved molecular packing in PDISNN, showing both shorter π–π stacking distances (d = 3.47 Å) and greater crystalline coherence lengths (CCL = 50.41 Å) compared to PDINN (3.58 Å, 41.35 Å) and PDI2SNN (3.60 Å, 43.12 Å) (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 1). The relative degree of crystallinity was quantified for the PDI-interlayer series, revealing values of 0.84, 1.00 and 0.87 for PDINN, PDISNN and PDI2SNN, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 7). These results confirm that the PDISNN interlayer possesses the highest crystallinity among the three materials. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations confirm that the enhanced crystallinity of PDISNN relative to PDI2SNN arises from its more planarity and asymmetric geometry induced by S-annelation (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 8). This structural modification affords a larger electrostatic molecular dipole moment (1.08 D vs 0.33 D for PDI2SNN)27 and yields a more favourable average interaction energy for the π–π stacked pairs (–24.39 kcal mol⁻1 in PDISNN vs –22.56 kcal mol−1 in PDI2SNN). This enhanced crystallinity coupled with a stronger self-doping effect (Fig. 1f) leads to an improved conductivity of 5.79 × 10−4 S cm−1 for PDISNN, compared to 4.95 × 10−4 S cm−1 for PDINN and 3.76 × 10−4 S cm−1 for PDI2SNN (Supplementary Fig. 9). These results demonstrate that S-heterocyclic annelation modifies intermolecular and intramolecular interactions make them promising candidates for cathode interlayers in OSCs, offering improved electron extraction and transport capabilities28,29.Device fabrication and performanceFor device fabrication, the S-heterocyclic PDIs were dissolved in 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (TFE) solvent to ensure proper solubility as they exhibit poor solubility in methanol. The reason for choosing TFE as solvent is that we drew inspiration from proteins, which exhibit an amphiphilic structure with both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions, a property similarly shared by interlayer materials. This similarity led us to hypothesize that TFE, a solvent effective in dissolving proteins, might also dissolve interlayers. As expected, S-heterocyclic PDIs readily dissolved in TFE (denoted as Method I, Fig. 2a), allowing for the formation of uniform thin films on the active layer. Modest PCEs of 14.78%, 14.98% and 14.59% were recorded for PDINN, PDISNN and PDI2SNN interlayers, respectively (Table 1). These low PCEs were primarily attributed to low open-circuit voltage (VOC) values of 0.81 V and fill factors (FFs) around 70%. Given the amphiphilic nature of the PDI interlayer, we investigated its potential for selective molecular contact with the active layer by incorporating an additional step: rinsing the interlayer surface with methanol (denoted as Method II). This adjustment yielded a slight improvement in device efficiency, primarily driven by an increased VOC of 0.83 V.Table 1 PM6: BTP-eC9-based binary solar cell performance using three PDI interlayers deposited by different methodsFull size tableWhen the active layer surface was pretreated with methanol (denoted as Method III), an intriguing phenomenon emerged regarding the interlayer’s surface wettability. This observation sparked our curiosity and prompted a deeper investigation into its impact on device performance. To elucidate the effect, we examined TFE droplets containing various PDIs on the active layer surface. Without methanol pretreatment, the contact angles for PDINN-, PDISNN- and PDI2SNN-TFE droplets were 28.0°, 29.4° and 29.7°, respectively. Methanol pretreatment, however, reduced these angles dramatically to 12.1°, 13.6° and 14.4° (Supplementary Fig. 10). The notable decrease demonstrated that methanol substantially improved the wetting behaviour of the active layer surface, enabling stronger interfacial contact with the TFE-based interlayer solution. Motivated by this discovery, we explored the impact of this methodology on device performance. The PDISNN-based device achieved a standout PCE of 18.25%, along with a substantially increased VOC of 0.85 V, FF of 78.40% and a JSC of 27.23 mA cm−2 (Fig. 2b; corresponding incident photon-to-electron conversion efficiency curves shown in Supplementary Fig. 11). Ellipsometry confirms a consistent PDI-interlayer thickness around 11 nm (Supplementary Fig. 12), and photo-induced force microscopy verifies homogeneous molecular distribution (Supplementary Fig. 13), collectively ruling out incomplete surface coverage as factors in performance differences. Similar enhancements were noted for PDINN- and PDI2SNN-based devices, underscoring the potential of this simple yet effective pretreatment method (Fig. 2c).With the success of our method, one potential concern is the low boiling point of methanol, which may affect the reproducibility of the device. Interestingly, we find that the device maintains a consistently high level of efficiency even when the TFE solution of PDISNN is spin coated after a 30-min delay following methanol pretreatment (Supplementary Fig. 14 and Supplementary Table 3). Fourier transform infrared attenuated total reflection spectroscopy confirms residual methanol via O–H (3,370 cm−1) and C–O (1,033 cm−1) stretching vibrations, characteristic of surface-adsorbed low-order methanol clusters (Supplementary Fig. 15)30. This observation indicates a broad processing window enabled by strong methanol adsorption on the active layer, which facilitates subsequent PDI-interlayer deposition.In addition to methanol, we also tried other alcohols, such as ethanol and isopropanol, as alternative pre- or post-treatment solvents on the device performance. The results suggest that ethanol was less potent than methanol, whereas isopropanol performed worse (Supplementary Fig. 16 and Supplementary Table 4). It is suggested that the polarity of alcohol appears to be a crucial factor, with methanol being the most desirable, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 16c.Interlayer assembly for enhanced interfacial dipoleTo better understand the underlying molecular-level interactions governing device performance, we performed sum-frequency generation (SFG) vibrational spectroscopy to probe the orientation of interlayer molecules. SFG is a second-order nonlinear technique that selectively probes surface and interfacial structures. SFG signals are acquired using a ssp polarization combination, that is, s-SFG, s-visible and p-infrared. The spectral intensity reflected the infrared dipole moment of vibration modes with a component perpendicular to the substrate31. We understand that the changes in the SFG signals can result from other factors, and hence we also complement our SFG measurements with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and structural characterizations.Our investigation began with the assembly behaviour of the benchmark interlayer PDINN to understand its high performance. Specifically, we focused on signals around 1,530–1,538 cm−1, corresponding to the C = C stretching vibrations of perylene in the excited state (Fig. 3a)32. These signals were nearly undetectable on the surface of the ITO and ITO/active layer (Supplementary Figs. 17 and 18). The angles between PDINN molecules and the surface normal were calculated based on experimental conditions, where lower values indicate a more perpendicular orientation to the active layer. When a PDINN methanol solution was directly deposited onto the active layer (PM6: Y6) via the conventional method, the calculated angle was 31.65° (Fig. 3b), yielding a good device efficiency of 16.46%. To explore the influence of surface properties on interlayer orientation, we pretreated the active layer with hexane to reduce its surface energy (Fig. 3c). This modification increased the calculated angle to 35.83°, indicating a less perpendicular orientation, which adversely reduced the device efficiency to 12.71% (Supplementary Table 5). This molecular-level insight underscores the critical interplay between surface properties and interlayer assembly in determining device performance.Fig. 3: Interfacial characterization.Full size imagea, SFG spectra of active layer surface, the inset illustrates the experimental geometry with PDI molecules cast on the active layer/ITO substrate; ωVIS (visible beam), ωIR (infrared beam) and ωSFG (sum-frequency output, ωVIS + ωIR) denote the angular frequencies in SFG spectroscopy. The ssp, sps and ppp polarization combinations denote s-/s-/p-, s-/p-/s- and p-/p-/p-polarized sum frequency, visible, and infrared beams, respectively. b, Active layer/PDINN surface. c, Active layer/n-hexane/PDINN. d, SFG spectra (ssp polarization) of CIL films deposited through different methods, fitted curves are plotted alongside the observed data points. e, Schematic illustration of the experimental set-up. f, Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) results of active layer surface coated with PDINN, PDISNN and PDI2SNN through Method I or Method III. g, Shifting of vacuum level obtained from KPFM results.Source dataFurthermore, as shown in Fig. 3d, we compared the SFG signals of different interlayers. PDI interlayers deposited with Method III demonstrate markedly stronger SFG signals at around 1,538 cm−1 compared to those deposited without pretreating with methanol (Method I). Therefore, Method III promoted the PDI molecules being preferred perpendicular to the substrate (more details in Supplementary Discussion). In addition, angle-dependent near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure showed that the average molecular orientation angles (α) were 74.54° (Method I), 78.38° (Method II) and 85.01° (Method III), respectively (Supplementary Fig. 19). The integrated pole files of GIWAXS also demonstrate that Method III dominates a notable increase in edge-on molecular orientation (Supplementary Fig. 19). The statistical distribution of molecular orientation angles at the interface is consistent with the SFG measurement results (Supplementary Note 1), indicating that methanol treatment promotes a preferential alignment of PDI-interlayer molecules with a more perpendicular orientation relative to the substrate.To gain a deeper understanding of the aromatic orientation in the two-step process, MD simulations were performed. In these simulations, PDISNN molecules were initially placed on the surface of both the pristine L8-BO film and the methanol-shrouded film (Supplementary Figs. 20 and 21 and Supplementary Discussion). A comprehensive model of tuning the PDI-interlayer molecular orientation was represented under the three different configuration states: single molecule, molecular clusters and multiple molecules (Supplementary Discussion). All analyses consistently demonstrated that the presence of methanol molecules on the surface of the BTP-eC9 film promoted a perpendicular orientation of the PDISNN molecules, with the amine-containing side chains extending out-of-plane.On the basis of the SFG results and molecular orientation insights from MD simulations, we propose two distinct arrangements of PDI molecules deposited via Method I and Method III. Considering that state-of-the-art active layers often feature polar functional groups such as halogens, cyano groups or carbonyl groups, the formation of hydrogen-bonding interactions between the active layer and methanol is plausible (Supplementary Fig. 15). These interactions are evidenced by an enhanced wettability of the active layer surface (Fig. 2a). In Method III, residual methanol on the active layer acts as a molecular template, guiding the self assembly of the PDI molecules. Due to its strong polarity, the residual methanol interacts preferentially with the polar side chains of the PDI molecules, promoting a more perpendicular orientation of PDI molecules during the film-forming process. This templating effect also influences the aggregation dynamics of the PDI molecules from solution to film and enhances the exposure of polar groups, particularly amines, on the surface of the PDI interlayer, thereby facilitating direct contact with the subsequently deposited Ag electrode. In contrast, Method II involves the post-deposition application of methanol to PDI interlayer whose morphology is already largely dried and fixed. At this stage, methanol penetration to the buried interface is severely limited, preventing it from effectively templating the PDI self assembly.The enhanced contact between the amines and electrodes is crucial for reducing the work function of the cathode. The pristine Ag, a widely used cathode, has a work function of 4.28 eV, which is notably higher than the quasi-Fermi level of photo-induced electrons (EF,e) in the acceptor of the active layer. This mismatch creates a substantial Schottky barrier28, hindering electron extraction and reducing VOC. DFT calculations (Supplementary Fig. 22) reveal that amine-containing side chains dramatically lower the work function of Ag to 3.11 eV, whereas the three aromatic cores (PDI, PDI-S and PDI-2S) have negligible influence. These findings suggest that a more perpendicular PDI-core orientation increases contact between amine groups and the electrode, effectively reducing the work function of metal electrodes for an increase in VOC.As is well known, the packing of interlayer molecules fundamentally affects the surface properties of the active layer. With a more perpendicular orientation of the PDI core, we are interested to know how the effect of this orientation influences the interfacial dipole. Thus, we employed scanning Kelvin probe microscopy to measure the surface potential of the active layer (Fig. 3e). For PDISNN deposited directly from TFE (Method I), the surface potential was approximately 192 mV higher than that of the bare active layer (Fig. 3f,g). Remarkably, after methanol pretreatment (Method III), this difference increased to 233 mV, demonstrating a notable enhancement. These findings align with reports by Cao and Hou et al.33,34. Similar trends were observed for PDINN and PDI2SNN-based CILs. This is further confirmed by the ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS), which shows that the work function of the active layer decreases from 4.26 eV for pristine active layer to 4.17 eV after Method III treatment (Supplementary Fig. 23). These results confirm that the stepwise deposition method markedly improves surface potential. Among the CILs, PDISNN exhibited the most positive surface potential, which we attribute to its asymmetric electrostatic potential (ESP) distribution across the aromatic core. The enhanced surface potential corresponds to a downward shift of the vacuum level, a key factor in facilitating efficient electron extraction at the active layer/interlayer interface.With increased surface potential, an enhanced built-in electric field and reduced transport resistance can be expected in devices20,33. To verify this, we analysed the built-in electric field of devices using the Mott–Schottky method (Supplementary Fig. 24). Device fabricated using Method III exhibited appreciably higher built-in potential (Vbi) values close to ~ 0.82 V, compared to the approximately 0.65 V observed for devices prepared using Method I. In addition, a sharp decrease in series resistance from 158.6 Ω (Method I) to 29.6 Ω (Method III) was revealed by impedance spectroscopy (Supplementary Fig. 25), revealing a reduced interfacial Schottky barrier with Method III (Supplementary Discussion)17,19,28. Overall, these combined effects mitigate interfacial charge accumulation, a primary source to trap-assisted non-radiative recombination. Thus, the perpendicular dipole orientation reduces non-radiative losses and thereby enhances the VOC (Supplementary Fig. 26 and Supplementary Table 6). In parallel, a combination of factors including reduced series resistance, enhanced charge carrier mobility (Supplementary Figs. 27 and 28), suppressed recombination under operating bias and diminished bias-dependent charge generation—synergistically contributes to the substantial FF enhancement observed in devices processed with Method III35.Universality of the interlayer and deposition methodWe further investigated the effectiveness of PDISNN deposited using this method on other active layers, including PM6:PY-IT, PM6:L8-BO and D18:L8-BO systems. Figure 4a presents the distribution plots of PCE values, with the corresponding device parameters summarized in Table 2. The J–V curves and incident photon-to-electron conversion efficiency of these devices are shown in Supplementary Fig. 29. The PCE surpasses that of devices using the classical interlayer PDINN and the D18:L8-BO active layer, which typically report PCE values in the range of 19.0–19.5% (refs. 36,37,38,39,40). Beyond the benefits of the methanol-templated PDISNN interlayer as discussed above, its favourable LUMO alignment with L8-BO (−3.83 eV vs −3.90 eV) creates a minimal barrier. This further suppresses interfacial recombination, thereby enabling an external quantum efficiency value approaching 90% at around 800 nm (Supplementary Fig. 29g). An independently certified PCE of 20.65% with a high FF of 82.7% was attained for our champion device (certified by National Center of Inspection on Solar Photovoltaic Products Quality; Supplementary Fig. 30). The high certified PCE and FF are among the highest values so far for any binary system (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Table 7), achieved solely through interlayer engineering.To evaluate scalability and stability, we fabricated 1 cm2 devices based on D18:L8-BO (Supplementary Fig. 31) that achieved a 19.20% PCE for binary systems, approaching the 19.32% benchmark of ternary devices41. Further, the Method III–based devices exhibited a T80 lifetime (time to 80% of initial PCE) of 984 h, substantially exceeding the 330 h observed for the control devices (Supplementary Fig. 32). This demonstrates the efficacy of Method III in mitigating scaling-induced series resistance losses and non-uniform charge collection. In addition, we applied our stepwise deposition method to other PDI-based CILs (Fig. 4d,e). Among these, PDINN-4Cl exhibits limited solubility in methanol and water, which posed challenges for conventional deposition. The results demonstrate that our method effectively enhances device performance in binary and in ternary devices (Supplementary Fig. 33 and Supplementary Table 8). This finding highlights the versatility of our approach for device fabrication, addressing solubility limitations associated with conventional techniques while improving overall device performance.ConclusionsIn this study, we develop a stepwise, methanol-templated film deposition strategy that precisely controls the packing orientation of cathode interlayer molecules while overcoming solubility limitations of conventional orthogonal deposition methods. Our study establishes that ordered PDI molecules, oriented perpendicular to the substrate, enhance the interfacial dipole, as evidenced by lowered work function and enhanced surface potential. This optimized interlayer reduces the interfacial Schottky barrier and enhances the built-in electric field with a reduced charge transport resistance. Consequently, the suppression of interfacial charge accumulation, a primary source of trap-assisted non-radiative recombination, is suppressed, leading to a marked increase in the open-circuit voltage and device efficiency. A certified PCE of 20.65% with a fill factor of 82.7% in binary OSCs using PDISNN is achieved. Moreover, the versatility of the stepwise deposition method is demonstrated across various interlayer materials, consistently achieving higher efficiencies than conventional methods. Overall, our results provide important guidelines for the future development of organic solar cells by emphasizing the critical role of interfacial molecular orientation.MethodMaterialsITO glass with a sheet resistance of 15 Ω sq−1 were purchased from Youxuan New Energy Technology Co. where \({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}\) represents the total surface energy of solid, composing of the dispersion force \({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{\,{\rm{D}}}\) and polarity force \({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{\,{\rm{P}}}\). \({\gamma }_{{\rm{l}}}\) represents the surface energy of the liquid and consists of a dispersion force \({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{\,{\rm{D}}}\) and polarity force \({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{\,{\rm{P}}}\).By measuring the contact angle (θ) of a testing liquid with known \({\gamma }_{{{l}}}^{\,{{D}}}\) and \({\gamma }_{l}^{\,P}\) on the solid film, the solid surface energy components can be determined using the following equation:$${\gamma }_{{\rm{l}}}\left(1+\cos \theta \right)={2\left({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{{\rm{D}}}{\gamma }_{{\rm{l}}}^{{\rm{D}}}\right)}^{1/2}+{2\left({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{{\rm{P}}}{\gamma }_{{\rm{l}}}^{{\rm{P}}}\right)}^{1/2}$$
(2)
To solve for \({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{\,{\rm{D}}}\) and \({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{\,{\rm{P}}}\), contact angles from two different testing liquids are required:$${\gamma }_{{\rm{l}}1}\left(1+\cos \theta \right)={2({\gamma }_{s}^{{\rm{D}}}{\gamma }_{{\rm{l}}1}^{{\rm{D}}})}^{1/2}+{2({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{{\rm{P}}}{\gamma }_{{\rm{l}}1}^{{\rm{P}}})}^{1/2}$$
(3)
$${\gamma }_{l2}\left(1+\cos \theta \right)={2({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{{\rm{D}}}{\gamma }_{{\rm{l}}2}^{{\rm{D}}})}^{1/2}+{2({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{{\rm{P}}}{\gamma }_{{\rm{l}}2}^{{\rm{P}}})}^{1/2}$$
(4)
Finally, the total surface energy of the solid is obtained by summing the dispersion and polar components: \({\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}={\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{\,{\rm{D}}}+{\gamma }_{{\rm{s}}}^{\,{\rm{P}}}\).Molecular dynamics simulationsThe simulations were conducted with GROMACS-2020.6 software package based on the GAFF force field (SoftwareX 2015, 1–2, 19–25). The atomic charges were derived using the restrained electrostatic potential fitting scheme with Multiwfn at the B3LYP/def2-TZVP level with Grimme’s D3 dispersion correction with BJ dampening. Equilibrium bond lengths and angles were updated based on B3LYP-D3BJ/6-31 G (d,p) optimized geometries. All the DFT calculations were performed using Gaussian 16 package. The details of MD procedure can be found in Supplementary Discussion.DFT calculationThe molecular DFT calculation were performed using Gaussian software with B3LYP function and the 6–31 G (d,p) basis sets27. The ESP and fragment dipole moments analysis were performed through Multiwfn software43. The work function (WF) calculations were carried out in the Dmol3 of Materials Studio. Generalized gradient approximation (GGA) was applied in the study of molecule–metal adsorption systems. The electronic structure of the model was described by the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) method.SFG measurementThe SFG measurements were carried out on the full device stack (ITO/active layer (PM6: Y6, 100 nm)/PDI interlayer (11 nm)) to ensure interfacial relevance to actual devices. The PDI molecular orientation angles were determined from the relative intensities of SFG signals under ssp, ppp and sps polarization combinations, using a well-established model and procedure44. The tilt angle θ was derived from the ratio of χ(2) tensor elements (for example, χssp/χppp), which relates to the mean orientation of the transition dipole moment, θ = f(Issp, Ippp). To quantify the uncertainty in the tilt angles, we applied standard error propagation theory to address experimental uncertainties. The tilt angle θ is calculated from the ratio of χ(2) tensor components (for example, χssp/χppp), and the error propagation follows the principle that the variance of θ (σ2θ) can be estimated using the partial derivative formula:$${{\rm\sigma }}_{{\rm\theta }}^{\,2}\approx {(\partial {{f}}/\partial {I}_{\mathrm{ssp}})}^{2}{{{\rm\sigma }}_{{I}_{\mathrm{ssp}}}}^{2}+{(\partial {{f}}/\partial {I}_{\mathrm{ppp}})}^{2}{{{\rm\sigma }}_{{I}_{\mathrm{ppp}}}}^{2}$$
(5)
where \({{\rm{\sigma }}}_{I}\) represents the standard deviation of the intensity measurements. The partial derivatives (\(\partial f/\partial {I}_{\mathrm{ssp}}\)) and (\(\partial f/\partial {I}_{\mathrm{ppp}}\)) quantify the sensitivity of the calculated θ to variations in the SFG intensity measurements. These derivatives are evaluated numerically or analytically depending on the functional form of f, which is typically nonlinear due to the trigonometric relationships involved in orientation analysis. The standard deviations were calculated from the variability in SFG intensity ratios, leading to tilt angles of 31.6 ± 1.9° for the conventional method (Method I) and 35.8 ± 1.2° for the hexane-pretreated case (as mentioned in the main text). The small uncertainties (for example, ± 1.2°–1.9°) demonstrate the reliability of the orientation analysis. Furthermore, the consistency of the tilt angles across different polarization combinations (ssp, ppp, sps) reinforces the validity of the model. For example, the ppp and sps polarizations provided complementary constraints on the orientation distribution, reducing potential artefacts from non-resonant backgrounds or coverage variations. This multi-polarization strategy aligns with best practices in SFG studies of interfacial molecular order A constant offset was added to the y-axis values for Method III in Fig. 3d to better visualize the changes.Device fabricationThe OSCs were fabricated with a structure of ITO/PEDOT: PSS (Poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate)) or 2PACz /active layer/PDI-CILs/Ag, following a well-established procedure26. The ITO glass was cleaned by sequential ultrasonic treatment in water, deionized water, acetone and isopropanol and then treated in an ultraviolet ozone cleaner (Ultraviolet Ozone Cleaner, Jelight Company) for 20 min. The PEDOT: PSS aqueous solution was filtered through a 0.45-µm filter and then spin coated on precleaned ITO-coated glass at 4,000 rpm for 30 s. The PEDOT: PSS film was annealed at 150 °C for 20 min in air to form a 30 nm film. When 2PACZ as used, it was spin coated with a concentration of 0.27 mg ml−1 in ethanol on top of ITO substrates at 3,000 rpm and then dried at 100 °C for 10 min. A solution of active layer was prepared by dissolving the materials in chloroform and then was spin coated at 4,000 rpm onto the PEDOT: PSS layer or 2PACZ-coated substrate. The active layer solution was prepared by dissolving the materials in chloroform and then was spin coated at 4,000 rpm onto the PEDOT: PSS layer or 2PACZ-coated substrate. The active layer was pretreated with methanol by spin coating 30 μl of methanol at 3,000 rpm (Method III). Thermal annealing (100 °C for 10 min) was performed on the active layer to remove residual chloroform and to control the morphology. Then trifluoroethanol solution of PDI-CILs (PDINN, PDISNN and PDI2SNN) at a concentration of 1.0 mg ml−1 was deposited on the active layer at 3,000 rpm for 30 s to afford a cathode buffer layer. As control experiments, the active layer was either directly deposited with PDI-CILs (Method I) or further post-treated with methanol (30 μl, spin coated at 3,000 rpm, Method II). Finally, the metal cathode Ag was thermal evaporated under a mask at a base pressure of ~10−5 Pa. The ternary device was fabricated following the same procedure as the binary device. The photovoltaic area of the device is 6 mm2. Optical microscope (Olympus BX51) was used to define the active area of the devices.Device characterizationThe J–V curves of the OSCs were measured in a nitrogen glove box with a Keithley 2450 Source Measure unit under illumination from a Solar Simulator (model, SS-X50, Enli Technology Co. Ltd.) equipped with an AM 1.5 filter. The light intensity was calibrated to 100 mW cm−2 by a certified reference silicon cell (certified by Enli Technology Co. Ltd.). The active area of the device was defined by the aperture masks as 0.0256 cm2 for the small-area device and 1 cm2 for the large-area device. The J–V scans were performed from −0.2 V to 1 V with a voltage step of 20 mV and a delay time of 1 ms. The external quantum efficiency was measured by Solar Cell Spectral Response Measurement System QE-R3-011 (Enli Technology Co. Ltd.), with light intensity at each wavelength calibrated by a standard single-crystal Si photovoltaic cell. Operational stability was conducted by using the white light LED array under continuous illumination of the simulating intensity of 100 mW cm−2 (spectral region: 410–850 nm, Suzhou D & R Instruments, PVLT-6001M-32A) at the maximum power point in air at approximately 25 °C. The maximum power point was calibrated by the measured J–V curves every hour. Encapsulated devices were used for the stability measurements.Reporting summaryFurther information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.
